opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a single moment. It was more of a slow accumulation that eventually became impossible to ignore.

I'd spent most of my life thinking I'd be a mathematician. I loved research, the feeling of sitting with a problem for weeks and then suddenly seeing the structure underneath it. So the default path was very clear: finish the PhD, do a postdoc, try for a faculty job. And that path is a beautiful one; I have enormous respect for people who take it.

But over the past couple of years I kept watching what was happening with AI reasoning, and I had this growing feeling that mathematics was about to change in a really fundamental way. Models were getting better at producing arguments, and formal proof systems like Lean were maturing at the same time. When you put those together, you can imagine a system that doesn't just *sound* right but can actually verify that it's right. To me that felt like one of the most important things one could work on, both for math itself and as a testbed for trustworthy reasoning in general.

So the question I kept asking myself was: where can this actually get built? Some of it can happen in academia, but the scale of compute, the engineering effort, the need to bring together mathematicians, formal methods people, and machine learning researchers in one room, all moving fast, that pointed toward a company.

There was also a timing element. I had this sense that the window was now. If I waited until I'd checked every box, finished the degree, gotten the perfect credentials, the most interesting phase would already be over. And I asked myself the classic question: when I'm older, would I regret trying this and failing, or regret not trying? The answer was very obvious once I framed it that way.

Of course I was scared. I talked to a lot of people: my advisors, friends who'd started companies, mathematicians I admire. Some were very supportive, some were skeptical, and both were useful. The skeptics helped me sharpen what I actually believed. In the end, I realized I wasn't really leaving mathematics. I was trying to build something that could serve mathematics, and that made the decision feel much less like a departure and much more like a continuation.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one clean decision. It was more like a slow accumulation of evidence that I couldn't ignore anymore.

I'd spent years in pure math, and I loved it. There's nothing quite like sitting with a problem for months and finally seeing why it has to be true. But somewhere around the time I was finishing at Stanford, I started feeling this gap between what I was doing and what I thought was possible. The tools we had for doing mathematics, for actually discovering and verifying things, hadn't really changed in decades. And meanwhile the models were getting good enough that I could imagine a world where that changed.

The question I kept asking myself was: who is going to build this? And every time I ran through the list, I didn't like the answer. The big labs would get to it eventually, but mathematics would be a side project for them. The academic groups cared deeply but didn't have the resources or the incentive to ship something real. So it kept coming back to, well, maybe it has to be people like me.

I also had a lot of conversations with people I trusted, including some who told me not to do it. That was useful. One of my mentors said something like, you can always go back to research, but you can't always go back to this moment. The timing felt specific. The models were just crossing a threshold, formal verification was mature enough to be useful, and there was a small window where someone with the right combination of math background and willingness to be a little reckless could actually do something.

The last piece was accepting that I wouldn't feel ready. I think I waited for a long time for some feeling of certainty that never came. At some point I realized that the discomfort wasn't a signal that I shouldn't do it. It was just what it feels like to do something you haven't done before. So I stopped treating it as a decision to be solved and started treating it as a bet to be made. And once I framed it that way, it got much easier.

astra-6.text:
For me, it came down to separating two questions: did I like the idea of starting a company, or was there a problem I wanted to work on enough that starting a company made sense? Those are quite different motivations.

I tried to make the decision concrete. What would I actually spend my days doing? What would I be giving up? And what could I learn by taking a first step, rather than trying to resolve every uncertainty in advance?

I don’t think you ever get complete confidence. At some point, you have to decide whether you’re willing to commit while still having unanswered questions. That was the shift for me—from needing to know it would work to being willing to find out.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it came down to separating two questions: did I want to start a company, and was there a problem I cared enough about to build a company around? Those are quite different. You can be attracted to the idea of being a founder, but that doesn’t necessarily give you a reason to keep going when the work gets difficult.

I don’t think you can resolve that entirely by thinking about it. You have to take some small steps—talk to people, test your assumptions, try to build something—and see whether you become more convinced as you learn.

So I wouldn’t describe it as reaching certainty. It was more deciding that the uncertainty was worth taking on, and that I wanted to give the idea a serious chance.
